entries.title: Southwest flood damage estimates are hundreds of millions for New Mexico alone
entries.summary: Intense rainstorms linked to a very active El Niño-driven Pacific hurricane season have left thousands of people in the Four Corners states displaced.
entries.content:
Southwest flood damage estimates are hundreds of millions for New Mexico alone

Intense rainstorms linked to a very active El Niño-driven Pacific hurricane season have left thousands of people in the Four Corners states displaced or facing massive cleanups from flooding.

The adjoining states of Colorado, New Mexico, Utah and Arizona all saw substantial flooding last week, and damage assessments are just starting to trickle in from cities, towns and some of the most remote territory in the continental U.S.

The northern New Mexico city of Farmington was hit particularly hard after torrential rains fell on the San Juan mountains in Colorado, sending floodwaters down the San Juan River that passes through Farmington on its way to Lake Powell on the Utah-Arizona border.

San Juan River saw some of biggest surges

Small towns all along the river, from Pagosa Springs, Colorado, to Bloomfield, New Mexico and Bluff, Utah all saw historic flooding and are now assessing recovery challenges.

About 46,000 people live in Farmington, long a center for coal, oil and natural gas production. It's also an important hub for the northeast side of the Navajo reservation, which sprawls across three states.

Farmington residents started getting evacuation notices on their phones as early as Wednesday night.

"My sister was notified on Thursday that she had to get out," said Connie Gooch, who has lived in Farmington for more than 65 years.

Gooch's sister owns a house in a suburban neighborhood near the San Juan River.

"Every year she goes through this," Gooch said. "The river starts rising, and she starts making sandbags to put around. But this year it was so fast she didn't have time to do that."

According to National Weather Service data from a river gauge in Farmington, the San Juan grew 13 times larger in just 36 hours, late last week.

In the wee hours of Thursday morning, the river was about 3.5 feet high. By Friday, it was 14 feet high, flooding neighborhoods across the city, and possibly setting a record for the highest water ever recorded in the city.

This even after the Navajo Reservoir upstream from Farmington was able to mostly contain water rushing down from the mountains. But downstream of the reservoir, flood surges into the city came from two normally dry tributaries, Gobernador Canyon and Cañon Largo.

"This is a catastrophic flood of historic proportions," said Devon Neeley, San Juan County's public information officer.

"This river got wider than we have ever seen it in our lifetimes."

From Colorado peaks to Arizona deserts

Similar reports are coming in from the other side of the San Juan mountains in Colorado.

"It's nothing like most of us have seen before," said Tyler Schmidt, captain of the fire and rescue team in the small town of South Fork, Colo. on the banks of the Rio Grande. "We had several neighborhoods that were under two to three feet of water."

Colorado Public Radio's Dan Boyce reports that responders' immediate priorities are lifting final evacuation orders as waters recede. Damaged bridges need to be assessed. Well water all down the Rio Grande's path in the San Luis valley needs to be tested.

Other drinking water impacts from the storm include sewage spills from flooded treatment plants in Sedona, Arizona and other locations. KNAU reports extensive damage on the Hopi reservation.

The Hopi reservation is surrounded by the Navajo reservation, where there have also been reports of rescues, washed out roads and flooding of historic proportions.

San Juan County, New Mexico's Neeley said fire crews, police officers, National Guard troops, and even out-of-state swift water teams rescued between 200 and 300 county residents.

"We have pulled people out of vehicles stuck in running washes. We have pulled people by helicopter off of rooftops," Neeley said. "We have used not only high-clearance vehicles from the National Guard, but amphibious vehicles because the water is so high. It's been a lot."

Some relief in the works

By Sunday, the rain had eased, river levels were falling, and some residents started returning home to assess flood damage.

Connie Gooch delivered tarps and other materials to her sister's house.

"The river was up four feet in her house," she said.

She found a neighborhood full of people moving furniture out of their homes and piling demolition debris in their front yards.

"There were trucks and cars all over the place," Gooch said. "There was a guy in front of me carrying a loaded trailer full of sheet rock that they'd chipped out of somebody's house."

But officials want the thousands of evacuated residents to stay out for now.

"The public is anxious to get back in; we recognize that, we're sympathetic to that," said San Juan County Fire Chief David Vega at a public briefing Sunday. "Now that the swift water component is out of the way, that exposes a whole new set of hazards for us," Vega added.

Public officials are concerned about hazards like raw sewage and damaged gas lines, live power lines, and the floodwater itself.

"The water is not healthy," Vega said. "Stay out of the water. Gas, diesel, pesticides, fertilizer, these are not things that you want on your clothes."

New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham visited San Juan County on Monday.

Grisham said that the damage to infrastructure alone could cost hundreds of millions of dollars.

"I hope we're only spending 30 to 40 million (dollars)," Lujan Grisham said, responding to recovery cost estimates from San Juan County manager Mike Stark.

"We think this could be closer to between 200 and 300 million (dollars)," Lujan Grisham said. "The environmental issues and the road issues and infrastructure issues alone, really are expensive."

Monday night, Governor Lujan Grisham released an announcement, stating that the federal government has "partially granted" New Mexico's request for an emergency declaration in response to the regional flooding. Yesterday, Lujan-Grisham signed executive orders making $8.25 million more in state funding available for flood response.

entries.title: Israelis vote in their highest numbers in decades in pivotal elections
entries.summary: Israelis voted in their highest numbers in decades in a tense national election on Tuesday to decide whether to stick with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's far-right coalition or change course.
entries.content:
Israelis vote in their highest numbers in decades in pivotal elections

Israeli voters turned out in their highest numbers in decades in a tense national election on Tuesday to decide whether to stick with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's far-right coalition or change course.

Netanyahu is in a tight race with his top rival, Gadi Eisenkot, a center-right former military chief of staff, according to early exit polls after voting ended at 10 p.m. local time.

But the final tally won't likely be known until Wednesday. Even then, if no bloc wins an outright majority, it may take days or weeks to find who will be Israel's next prime minister as party leaders try to assemble a governing coalition.

Israelis consider this one of their most consequential votes in history — the first parliamentary election since the October 2023 Hamas-led attack and years of war in Gaza and elsewhere in the Middle East.

The exit polls didn't show a clear winner as they were broadcast on Israeli TV channels. They suggested Netanyahu's Likud Party received more votes than Eisenkot's Yashar party. But the final results will depend on the math and negotiations of broader alliances.

Opposition leaders quickly reacted to the results saying they suggested voters dealt a blow to Netanyahu's coalition.

"This is a very good outcome for Eisenkot" and his recently formed party, said Shira Efron, an expert at the Rand Corp. think tank. "The most likely scenario is that he will receive the mandate from the president to form the government," she told NPR. She said he could try to form a minority government or join an alliance with Arab politicians.

The voter turnout appeared on track to be the highest in nearly 40 years, according to election officials.

Enthusiasm was especially high among voters seeking to replace Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, with almost two decades in office across multiple tenures.

" Important is an underestimation, because it's much more than important. It's crucial," voter Naama Aaronsohn said of the election. "I'm worried. ... What's going to become of our country if there's not a major change?"

Another voter, Itamar Ariel, said there are problems in Israel but no one can replace Netanyahu. He said his choice is about security for Israel.

Netanyahu voiced alarm throughout the day, in a number of social media posts, commenting on the high number of Arab citizens of Israel who were turning up at the polls. Netanyahu urged his right-wing supporters to vote.

Nur Abu Na, a 30-year-old nurse, called Netanyahu's government racist against Arab citizens and said she believes it's important for the her Arab community to vote. There are two predominantly Arab parties in the elections.

"This government it's not good for us and ... not good for anyone," she said.

President Trump publicly endorsed Netanyahu. After going to war together against Iran, in June 2025 and again this February, the two leaders plan to launch major attacks against Iran after the Israeli and U.S. midterm elections.

This is a developing story and may be updated.

Daniel Estrin reported from Tel Aviv, Israel. Ruth Sherlock reported from Jerusalem. Samantha Balaban, Itay Stern, Shir David and Alon Avital contributed reporting in Israel.

entries.title: The Ebola outbreak is breaking records -- and just marked a grim milestone
entries.summary: The current outbreak, first identified in the Democratic Republic of Congo, has now counted 10,000 patients and has spread with great speed. How can it be stopped?
entries.content:
The Ebola outbreak is breaking records — and just marked a grim milestone

The fastest spreading Ebola outbreak in history has surpassed another grim milestone. More than 10,000 people have been infected since the outbreak was first declared in May, according to the latest government figures from the Democratic Republic of Congo.

"It's a milestone that we're all surprised to be passing this quickly," says Katie Thomas-Canfield, interim Ebola response director for the International Rescue Committee. "10,000 people affected by Ebola in such a short period is really staggering," she says, noting that at this point in the West Africa outbreak of 2014-2016, only about 4,000 people had been infected. But that earlier outbreak still has the highest case count — more than 28,000 cases.

The current outbreak is also the largest ever in geographic scope, spanning Nigeria to Kenya. It is second in the death toll, with nearly 5,000 deaths compared to the previous toll of over 11,000.

About a third of those who've died in this outbreak have been kids. Children under 5, with their developing immune systems, are hit especially hard — roughly three out of four infected have died.

"Behind every figure is a life interrupted, a family mourning, a health worker under pressure and a community seeking reassurance," said Mohamed Janabi, regional director for the World Health Organization Africa, at a press conference last week. "We must reach people earlier, bring safe care closer, and strengthen trust before fear becomes a barrier to survival."

Here's a look at some of the key questions about the 2026 outbreak.

Why has the outbreak become so bad so fast?

Part of the answer lies in uncertainty over when the virus started circulating

While the outbreak was officially declared in May, more recent evidence suggests the virus likely started spreading in February or March.

"That's a really long time for things to be undetected in communities, and that means we started at a disadvantage," says Thomas-Canfield. A confluence of factors contributed to the delay.

First, there's the fact that a rarer species of Ebola is behind the outbreak — Bundibugyo. Existing tests weren't calibrated for this species, leading to delays. What's more, this region of northeastern DRC is remote and beset by conflict. And U.S. cuts to foreign aid may have slowed disease surveillance efforts, says Nahid Bhadelia, an infectious disease physician at Boston University.

In those early days, "the writing was on the wall that this would be a hard road and it would need international cooperation," says Bhadelia. International cooperation and support have been slower in coming than in previous Ebola outbreaks.

In 2014, for example, healthcare workers from around the globe traveled to West Africa to bolster the response. Bhadelia was one of them.

"I think you are seeing a lot less American or other healthcare workers coming into DRC because of U.S. policy that Americans may not be allowed back even if they're sick," says Bhadelia. That's different from the policy in the prior major outbreak. "That means that a lot of the burden is being carried by DRC and regional healthcare workers."

Despite pledges of funding from around the world, including more than $880 million from the U.S., some health workers on the ground say that money is slow to materialize. "The scale of financing that's available for this response is really a fraction of what it was in our previous response," says Thomas-Canfield. "I think the degree of international solidarity has been a lot less."

Are we making progress?

The response on the ground has improved over the past several months. There are now two dozen or so diagnostic labs and more than 50 treatment centers.

"We're up toward almost 2,000 treatment beds for Ebola, so there's been a lot of progress," says Douglas Noble, global incident manager for Ebola at UNICEF. Nonetheless, roughly two-thirds of deaths are occurring in the community, not in treatment centers — a sign that people are not coming forward with symptoms. That figure has been stubbornly constant for months and needs to improve for the outbreak to get under control, says Noble.

Part of why people aren't seeking care may be that Bundibugyo infections can seem mild at first. "Things like fever, headache, body ache, they're all symptoms of the most common and largely treatable endemic diseases in the region," says Thomas-Canfield. Those who are infected with Ebola may not decide to seek treatment until it's too late, he says.

A bigger hurdle, say many healthcare workers on the ground, is community distrust.

An October survey from the International Rescue Committee found that 85% of respondents in North Kivu — a current hotspot — say that distrust of community responders is keeping them from seeking care.

"We're constantly fighting different kinds of rumors, different kinds of misinformation," says Thomas-Canfield of the International Rescue Committee. Many community members question whether Ebola is real or believe responders are just trying to make money. Others wonder why teams come for Ebola and not other diseases that afflict the region, like malaria or typhoid.

Community health workers are working hard to rebuild that trust. "I do think that in areas where we've been able to establish a longer-term presence, we're better able to respond," says Thomas-Canfield. But the virus is rapidly spreading to new health zones. Building trust from scratch is hard, she says. That's especially true in conflict zones, where fighting makes it hard to work, and armed groups actively sow disinformation.

When trust is low, people don't seek care or engage with health officials trying to find new cases and isolate their contacts. Roughly 80% of new cases are still coming in from people who weren't on health officials' radar. Until that rate goes down, the outbreak will remain out of control, says infectious disease doctor Bhadelia.

She points to the cases in Nigeria and Kenya this month as proof of that point. "The sporadic cases that we're seeing in neighboring countries is a sign of the growth in DRC," she says. While daily case counts seem to be plateauing, she says there's likely many regions where the virus is spreading undetected. "It's so far out of control."

Is there any hope that an Ebola vaccine or better treatments could tamp down numbers?

No vaccine or treatment is licensed for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola. Several are in the works, but all far from being used in this response.

There is an existing vaccine for Ebola. It's called Ervebo, but it targets a different species of the disease. It hasn't been widely deployed, but healthcare workers began receiving the vaccine in late August and researchers just started a clinical trial, dubbed Tumaini after the Swahili word for hope, aimed at testing how well Ervebo works against Bundibugyo. If it proves effective, "that would be amazing, that could make a difference," says Bhadelia. But she cautions that vaccines and new treatments are not a silver bullet.

"Targeted medical countermeasures are necessary, but they are not sufficient," she says. These interventions need to be coupled with basic public health measures, like tracing all the contacts for a newly infected person and isolating and treating those who are stricken. Improving these strategies takes more work and resources, she says, and she worries that the needed support may not come fast enough.

"In this moment, the question that scares me more than anything is will the international community turn its eyes and forget about DRC?" she says. "I am worried the funding will dry out, that we will not keep paying attention to a public health disaster that is much deeper and bigger in this moment than people realize."

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

entries.title: A judge halted D.C. golf course renovations. Trump says they'll still start next month
entries.summary: A federal judge has barred the government from clearing more trees or making other alterations to D.C.'s East Potomac Park without proper notice. Trump says his administration will appeal.
entries.content:
A judge halted D.C. golf course renovations. Trump says they'll still start next month

After weeks of tense hearings and late-night court filings, a federal judge has temporarily blocked the Trump administration from making any further alterations to East Potomac Park, the municipal D.C. golf course that the president wants to redevelop into a championship-level venue.

The long-simmering legal battle kicked into high gear in recent weeks, after the government cut down 430 trees on the golf course with less than a day's notice. That prompted a pair of lengthy court hearings that at times turned heated, with government officials repeatedly insisting that the tree-clearing was unrelated to the renovations President Trump had touted on social media. They contradicted the president's own social media posts from that very morning by saying there was no final plan for those renovations at all.

"Rarely, if ever, has the United States Department of Justice urged a federal court not to believe the sitting president," U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes wrote in her 70-page opinion. "And yet, here we are."

Reyes extended what was initially a two-week halt to tree removal, ordering the government not to cut down "or substantially prune or otherwise damage or impair" any trees at East Potomac Park without a court order. She also ordered it to provide "no less than ten business days' written advance notice" before closing or making any "irreversible modification" to any parts of the park while the legal battle plays out.

"By issuing this preliminary injunction, the Court does not end the round: it simply marks the ball until the parties can fully and fairly litigate this case," Reyes wrote.

Monday's ruling is a win for the D.C. Preservation League and a pair of local golfers who sued to prevent renovations earlier this year — and for the growing grassroots movement to protect the municipal course and the surrounding recreational area, which is beloved by runners, cyclists, birders and others.

"We are grateful the court intervened to stop the Trump-Vance administration's greed and lawlessness while the case continues, and we are eager to argue the case in court," said Skye Perryman, the president of the nonprofit Democracy Forward, which is representing the plaintiffs.

In a Truth Social post late Monday, Trump said the Department of the Interior will appeal the ruling. NPR has reached out to the Department of Interior but did not hear back in time for publication.

Trump also doubled down on his earlier announcement that construction will begin on Nov. 15 and keep the park closed for 15 months, adding that the "judge has absolutely no right to hold up this very important and beautiful Project."

"To have to give advanced notices to a judge who has no expertise in Golf, Architecture, Landscaping, Construction, or anything else having to do with building such a World Class Project, is not fair, appropriate, or Constitutional," Trump wrote.

Reyes herself has said she is not interested in policing the federal government's landscaping efforts.

That's why, as she explained in Monday's opinion, she repeatedly declined to intervene in the case — instead issuing repeated warnings against any unannounced major alterations — until "the Government did what it assured all it would not do."

"The Court earlier stated, 'I am not the Lorax. I do not speak for the trees,'" Reyes concluded. "The Court still does not speak for the trees. It speaks only for the rule of law."

On Tuesday afternoon, Reyes made a record of Trump's post and gave the government about 24 hours to clarify whether a plan exists to close East Potomac in mid-November and, if so, "how that can be reconciled" with what its lawyers previously told the court. She said she will schedule a status hearing for either Friday or Monday.

The judge took aim at the government's contradictions

Reyes' strongly-worded 70-page opinion came exactly a week after a seven-hour hearing in which she clashed repeatedly with the government's lawyers. She had already rejected the administration's request to recuse herself from the case because of alleged bias.

Last week's hearing featured sworn testimony from several officials from the Department of the Interior and National Park Service, to provide a fuller account of the origins and purpose of the controversial tree-clearing. But it teed up bigger questions about whether the administration had misled the court and the public over its intentions for the golf course.

"This started as a case about golf. That good walk spoiled. But it has become much more," Reyes wrote on Monday. "It now forces the Court to reconcile assertions by President Donald J. Trump with the sworn testimony of multiple government employees and the argument of senior Department of Justice attorneys."

Much of Reyes' opinion examines the gap between what Trump has said publicly and what his administration has told the court.

The most notable: Trump posted online the morning of last week's hearing that work would begin on the golf course "immediately." But hours later, in the courtroom, administration officials said in sworn testimony that they were not aware of any final plan.

Weaving together timelines and testimonies, Reyes ultimately agreed with plaintiffs that there does seem to be a golf course renovation plan (they refer to it as the "Washington National Plan") despite the administration's repeated denials.

"To be sure, the Court cannot pinpoint the exact date at which the Plan became final," Reyes wrote. "But it determines without hesitation that it occurred at some point well before October 15, 2026."

She doesn't accept the government's explanation that it cleared hundreds of healthy, non-invasive trees on such short notice to enact vegetation recommendations from a 2019 National Park Service Report (whose other recommendations, including for the city's other two municipal golf courses, went largely unaddressed in the last seven years). She called that justification "pretextual."

She took particular aim at the credibility of one witness, Gregory Wischer — a deputy chief of staff at the Interior Department — who was photographed carrying rolled-up concept plans while accompanying Trump and golf course architect Tom Fazio on a tour of East Potomac in June.

"Yet Wischer maintains that he — as Deputy Chief of Staff to the Secretary of the Interior — just spontaneously became interested in tree and vegetation management. In mid September. At the East Potomac Golf Course," Reyes wrote.

Reyes said the government "has made no compelling factual rebuttal." At one point, the administration accused the plaintiffs of conjecture "based on a handful of tweets." Reyes shut that down in Monday's opinion.

"The 'handful of tweets' are not complaints about the Red Sox's latest blown lead in the ninth. They are statements from the President of the United States, and from the Secretary of the Interior, about actions within their purview," she wrote. "And the posts say, in no uncertain terms, that a plan exists and that construction will start imminently — one even contains a final schematic of the Course's redesign."

What's next for East Potomac?

Trump said as recently as Monday night that he believes the renovations do not require approval. But, as Reyes pointed out in her opinion, administration officials acknowledged in a July hearing that major renovations would require federal environmental and historic preservation reviews.

Last week, however, administration lawyers presented an "alternative argument" that the renovations actually cannot be reviewed under the Administrative Procedure Act.

"It says, Emily Litella-style: 'Never mind,'" Reyes wrote, referring to the perpetually about-facing Saturday Night Live character. "But parties cannot change course whenever and however the evidence suits them … And so the Court does not credit this new argument."

Plaintiffs in the lawsuit argue that the government is purposefully approaching the golf course renovations as smaller projects — like dumping debris from the White House East Wing demolition last year or cutting down hundreds of trees this month — to avoid federally required environmental reviews.

That argument seems to hold water with Reyes, who said, the Interior Department likely violated the National Environmental Protection Act "by impermissibly segmenting its review of the Plan's environmental effects."

Monday's ruling — and the administration's promised appeal — could slow that process even more. Trump said on social media that work "must begin, immediately, if it is to be completed in a timely and seasonal manner."

But there are still many questions about the final product.

The rendering Trump shared earlier this month shows the park's three courses of varying ability levels combined into one that overtakes the entire peninsula, seemingly removing the perimeter road that runners and bikers use every day and raising questions about whether the historically affordable golf course could soon be less accessible.

Trump said Monday the redeveloped course will be able to host events like the PGA Championship and Ryder Cup, but will also be "open to the Public, at a reduced rate for those living in Washington, D.C."

The project is one of many ways he's looking to make his mark on the nation's capital, from building the White House ballroom to adding his name to the Kennedy Center to pushing through plans for a triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery.

entries.title: Bolsonaro's party accepts Brazil election defeat, but he refuses to concede
entries.summary: Brazil's opposition party accepts President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's election victory, but Flávio Bolsonaro won't concede, while President Trump calls the vote "rigged" without offering evidence.
entries.content:
Bolsonaro's party accepts Brazil election defeat, but he refuses to concede

BRASILIA, Brazil — Brazil's Liberal Party, the party of defeated presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, has acknowledged the results of Sunday's presidential election, recognizing incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's victory. But Bolsonaro himself has yet to formally concede defeat.

The party's president, Valdemar Costa Neto, said in a statement Monday that the party recognizes the election results but believes "questions raised about the vote" still need to be clarified.

The concession came as President Trump questioned the election's legitimacy, telling reporters Monday, "I didn't take sides, but it looked like another rigged election." Trump offered no evidence of fraud.

Bolsonaro initially said he would seek to annul the election results, citing alleged irregularities, including a last-minute extension of voting hours.

On Sunday, the Supreme Court ordered polling stations to remain open for two additional hours, until 7 p.m., following an appeal by Lula's campaign, which cited public transportation disruptions. Bolsonaro's campaign also requested an extension, citing heavy rain in southern Brazil.

In a video posted Monday, Bolsonaro shifted his approach, saying he would seek to have Lula's election victory disqualified over alleged abuses of political and economic power. "The law must apply to everyone," he said. "The competition must be fair and equal, which did not happen." Bolsonaro did not provide any evidence for this claim.

Bolsonaro also said Brazil's Federal Police had ordered him to surrender his passports after he visited his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, in Brasília.

The former far-right president is under house arrest after being sentenced to 27 years in prison for his role in the 2022 coup attempt against Lula.

"I was ordered right on the street to hand over my passports, and I'm also prohibited from leaving the country," he said in the video. Bolsonaro said the order was based on remarks by his brother Eduardo, who lives in the U.S., suggesting he should leave Brazil if he lost the election. The passport order was issued by Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes in connection with a separate investigation.

Lula won just over 51% of the valid votes, or approximately 64.2 million, compared with more than 48%, or nearly 59.8 million, for Bolsonaro.

The result marked a major comeback for Lula, who trailed his challenger in the first round, and put the breaks on a run of right-wing electoral victories in Latin America.

Lula's victory celebrations rang out across Brazil on Sunday night. Near downtown Rio de Janeiro, supporters hugged, shouted and sang the national anthem. Gains in major cities, including Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo, helped Lula overcome his first-round defeat, along with support from younger, older and working-class voters.

In his victory speech in São Paulo, Lula singled out young people who had helped mobilize support for his campaign.

"I wanted to thank the Brazilian people for the generosity they have shown me for a long time," he said. "And in this second round, I want to thank the Brazilian youth for their generosity in taking to the streets. They took to the streets to defend democracy in the country."

17-year-old Brisa Pereira cast her first vote at a busy polling place in one of Brasília's sprawling suburbs. She said Lula's journey from poor factory worker to president had inspired her. She also wanted to send a message to Trump and what she described as his push to dominate Latin America.

"It's not the '90s anymore. We have rights, and Donald Trump can't speak for all of America," Pereira said.

Lula had to win over voters across different demographic and geographic groups to defeat Bolsonaro. He gained more than 10 million additional votes compared with the first round, helped by increased turnout and support from voters who had backed other candidates or had previously stayed away from the polls.

"No wonder pollsters said a Lula victory was almost impossible," said Thiago Vidal, a political analyst with Prospectiva consultants.

"This was a nationwide victory, a systemic victory — from top to bottom, and from left to right," Vidal said.

The decisive margin gives Lula a mandate to govern, Vidal said, but the next four years will be challenging. Bolsonaro's Liberal Party made significant gains in Congress, leaving Lula facing a conservative opposition and a deeply divided electorate.

Vidal said Lula also learned important lessons about communicating with voters, particularly through social media. The president, who had relied more heavily on traditional media, embraced a more digital campaign in the final weeks.

"Part of that has to do with communication, and part of that therefore has to do with Lula, setting aside the traditional media and becoming more digital," Vidal said.

Much of that shift was credited to André Janones, a congressman from the bellwether state of Minas Gerais who helped direct Lula's online campaign. Janones used Instagram and WhatsApp to reach younger voters and mobilize supporters. His WhatsApp channel, dubbed "Lula's Army," attracted over 10 million followers.

In an election-night Instagram post, Janones captured the spirit of the celebrations with a message summing up the campaign: "Nothing is more powerful than when the people unite."

entries.title: Discursive Verses: Jay-Z, the Super Bowl and playing with house money
entries.summary: NPR Music culture critic and reporter Rodney Carmichael ruminates on the latest in rap culture. This week: Is the rap mogul's self-selection a crowning achievement or a final affront?
entries.content:
Discursive Verses: Jay-Z, the Super Bowl and playing with house money

It's no small irony that Jay-Z, the best personification of hip-hop's hopes and dreams, built his success by emulating America's worst excesses. Avarice. Greed. Domination. In turn, we idolized him for showing us "how to move in a room full of vultures." The streets he hustled in were made savage by design. The industry he conquered was out to vanquish him first. Indoctrinated by the same vampiric systems, we learned to praise those willing to sacrifice humanity — whether theirs or others' — in order to scale from the bottom up. The oppressor-oppressed dialectic can be funny that way. If you're not careful, you start to become the monster you're running from.

According to an announcement from the NFL, Jay-Z will headline the 2027 Super Bowl halftime show in February. He's reached a new pinnacle. Not the first rapper to play the halftime show, but the first act with the power to plug himself into that highly coveted slot. The gig even came with a $25 million paycheck, if you count the 2019 deal his entertainment agency Roc Nation scored to book the NFL's annual Super Bowl lineup. The game is to be sold, as the saying goes. And this time, a true player got to set the rules of engagement. After seven years of curating the talent — and pushing rap to the forefront in unprecedented fashion — he's poised to stick the proverbial feather in his Yankees fitted. Yet, hip-hop's response has been ambivalent. Some of us don't know whether we want to slow clap or slapbox with the god.

Whether it's viewed as a crowning achievement or the culmination of a deal that made Jigga the perfect "Black face" to whitewash the NFL's sullied image — per Colin Kaepernick's recent recounting (comments Jay-Z has not responded to) — ultimately depends on which version of the story hip-hop's most valuable hustler can convincingly sell. Like water to a whale.

Fresh off a PR crisis himself, Jay-Z's been engaged in his own rebranding campaign this year. It follows the recently recanted rape allegations made in a civil lawsuit that named Jay-Z and Sean "Diddy" Combs as co-defendants. (Jay-Z vehemently denied the allegations from the start and pursued a defamation and extortion lawsuit against the filing attorney, Tony Buzbee, which was also recently dismissed by an appellate court. Combs also denied the allegations against him and was sentenced to more than four years in prison on prostitution-related charges.) Surviving such a public smear campaign lent new meaning to the 30th anniversary of Reasonable Doubt. "We played enough defense, 2026 is all offense," as he told GQ's senior associate editor Frazier Tharpe in March. So he brought back the umlauts over his chosen name. He sheared off the Basquiat locs grown for both his daughter, Blue Ivy, and his deceased uncle. And he sold out Yankee Stadium three nights in a row.

But he's nobody's sellout.

That was the underlying message of his anti-protest freestyle on night one. With smug confidence, he responded to the backlash for making his vinyl reissue available exclusively at Target in the middle of a grassroots Black boycott to combat the retailer's DEI policy reversal.

"They say I sold out. Yeah, I did sell out. Three nights. I sold Yankee Stadium the hell out," he rapped a capella as a prelude to "Politics As Usual."

There's this erroneous idea that Jay-Z's image rehab is oddly out of character. It's bolstered by the belief that he's always been oblivious to what the general public thinks. He can afford to be. But the truth is he's always been keenly aware and blatantly responsive to critique — whether cultural or personal in nature. When he likened himself to "Che Guevara with bling on / I'm complex" on "Public Service Announcement (Interlude)," it was in direct response to former Village Voice and Vibe journalist Elizabeth Méndez Berry, who provoked him to consider the contradictions he laid bare by donning a diamond-encrusted Jesus piece atop a t-shirt featuring the Cuban revolutionary's face. "The piece was smacking Che Guevara upside the head," Méndez Berry recently told The Ringer's Joel Anderson. "Communism and capitalism colliding with every step."

When Harry Belafonte called out Jay and Beyoncé by name in 2012 and 2013 to criticize Black celebrities for "turn[ing] their back on social responsibility," Jay clapped back. "My presence is charity," he said in an interview with hip-hop journalist Elliott Wilson. His response also showed up in criminal justice reforms he pushed to address disproportionate rates of incarceration in the Black community. Even Decoded, his 2010 book written with dream hampton, was a first-person explainer meant to contextualize his lyrics with the liner notes of his lived experience.

His latest explanatory foray, the eight-episode HBO documentary Jay-Z in 8, pairs him with former Def Jam founder and producer/guru Rick Rubin. Appropriately set in the austere environs of France's former stock exchange, they sit across from one another for deep listening sessions of Jay's discography meant to trigger revelations. He covers the Che Guevara moment again. He talks about what it meant to confront his dad — who abandoned the family when Jay was 11 — just one month before his death. They talk generational trauma and family secrets. He even fills in some unredacted details from his hustling era. Mostly, he tics and bobs his head to the beat like rap's Rainman, shuffling through stored volumes of lyrics famously composed and committed to memory without ever having touched a pen.

No one does this dance between dualities better. Encoding performances for those who lived it. Translating rhymes for those consuming from a privileged distance. This Duboisian double consciousness is what makes him such an articulate marketer of the American Dream, a propaganda artist for Black excellence and capitalist exploits.

For Jay, crossing over didn't come through rapping. It came through his extracurricular moves. The brand sponsorships. The lucrative partnerships. Essentially, he became a cultural broker. The gatekeeper handing the key for entry over to the highest bidder. He played a key role in unlocking the Nets-NBA deal for developer Bruce Ratner that made Barclays Center the catalyst for gentrifying Brooklyn. Jay gained a minority ownership stake (.067 percent); longtime Brooklynites got displaced. He gave cover for Roger Goodell and the NFL to sidestep Colin Kaepernick's protests on behalf of Black America. The league's billionaire owners got a pass; racial injustice got performative slogans and empty charitable initiatives.

"Over and over, Jay is the one that powerful whites use to quiet Negro protests so they can make more money together," former hip-hop journalist Touré recently said, likening Jay-Z to a house Negro who repeatedly aligns himself with the white power structure while claiming to represent Black folks' come-up. The same conclusion is drawn by prominent video essayist F.D Signifier, who categorizes Jay-Z as part of the "Black misleadership class."

But the biggest condemnation actually comes from Jigga himself. In the final episode of Jay-Z in 8 — the documentary he co-executive produced — Jay also calls out so-called race hustlers and house Negroes who act as "extortionists" that "go to one place and say: You want our support? Give us the money." It's as if he doesn't realize how much his own actions resemble the behavior he's side-eyeing. "We['re] not getting it as a race together," he says. "We're slowly getting there separately, but it's not a concerted effort of us to align our powers and our finances to benefit our community."

We could blame Jay, but as he once rapped on "P.S.A.," he didn't invent the game. He "just rolled the dice, trying to get some change." When he hits that Super Bowl halftime stage at SoFi Stadium next year, he'll be playing with a pocketful of house money.

entries.title: A 'Green Army' is out to thwart El Niño flooding
entries.summary: In Nairobi, a city prone to floods, workers in the "Green Army" are making preparations to prevent disaster when El Niño arrives.
entries.content:
A 'Green Army' is out to thwart El Niño flooding

Nairobi is a city of rivers, streams and almost six million people.

For weeks, Kenya's bustling capital has braced for potentially catastrophic floods, as forecasters predict the strongest El Niño event on record this winter. Globally, this year's Super El Niño will likely peak in November or December and continue into early 2027. But Nairobi isn't just watching and waiting.

On a sunny October day near the city center, a team of workers in reflective vests shovels dirt and clears debris from the bank of a river. It's unseasonably hot — and hot days usually suggest there's an unusually strong rainy season ahead.

"The best thing to do is to be prepared," says Alex Oyando, a 30-year-old worker. "These drainage troughs are full of different things. When we remove the dirt, the water can flow — and it prevents flooding."

Nairobi frequently experiences catastrophic flash floods. More than 100 people died during rain-induced flash floods last March, and residents have pressured Kenya's government to do more to prevent these disasters in the future.

Reporting for El Niño duty

As part of the preparations, Nairobi's county government has mobilized the "Green Army," a youth-employment program of more than 4,000 people. While generally assigned to trash pickups and city greening projects, the workers have been out in full force to prepare for El

Niño, clearing drainages and dismantling illegal structures like food stalls. These buildings are generally constructed by the community without government permits and are at an increased risk of collapsing during natural disasters.

Earlier this month, Oyando and his colleagues widened a drainage ditch that runs along a busy road lined with stalls selling clothing. Piles of fabric, plastic bottles and other litter often build up in the stream, triggering flash floods.

While the pay isn't as much as he could make elsewhere, Oyando admits, the shifts are manageable and not too grueling.

"It's something that gives me an opportunity to make a living," he says.

Many of Oyando's colleagues live or grew up in Nairobi's low-income neighborhoods, which are the hardest hit by flash floods. Aging drainage infrastructure and clogged waterways can cause stormwater to build up. When it rains, he says, it's not unusual for his street to fill with water and flood his home.

"The infrastructure we've had in place for decades was tailored for a population of not more than 2 million people," says Bramwell Simiyu, the chief officer of disaster management for Nairobi's county government. "We're now talking about a daytime population of close to 7 million."

A $385 million remedy

Kenya's federal government has put in place a $385 million plan to widen Nairobi's waterways, build affordable housing and improve the city's trash pickup and sewer system by the end of 2027. In addition, the program supports a national youth employment program called Climate WorX, which is working with the Green Army on El Niño preparations.

Now, Simiyu says, the county is preparing supplies and evacuation centers for the rainy season.

"We're also preparing for a worst-case scenario, where up to about 20,000 households may be affected — mostly in the low -income settlements," Simiyu said.

Controversial demolitions

In these settlements, the demolition of illegally built structures, such as food hawker stalls, has caused an outcry. Tobias Sifuna, a supervisor for Green Army teams in the Kamukunji area of Nairobi, says it's a necessary step.

"These are small kiosks that are built illegally, by the community — without the authorization from the county government," Sifuna said.

But nearby communities rely on them, for income and for daily shopping.

Wycliffe Ochieng, a 32-year-old fruit vendor, says many workers in central Nairobi now have nowhere to buy an affordable hot lunch during the day.

"Now, we have to sleep without food because we can't afford it," Ochieng says.

When the county government destroys the shops, it's the community that feels the loss — whether or not the floods eventually come. But it's these neighborhoods that were hit the hardest by the floods during the last rainy season. Ochieng himself had to sleep outdoors, because he could not reach his home in the floodwaters.

"This place, it's like an ocean when it's raining," Ochieng says. "When the flood came, all the food stalls were swept away."

His friend, a woman who owned a food stall, died as she tried to escape. He lost his own stand, a small grocery, as well. He struggled to rebuild his business in a new neighborhood, where customers no longer knew him by reputation.

"After the flood I really suffered. It was hard to put food on the table," Ochieng says.

He says he hopes the county can do more to prevent flooding and safeguard livelihoods. There are only so many times he can rebuild his life from scratch.

"We are all scared. I fear if El Niño comes, I won't come back again."

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

entries.title: Democrats have a midterm edge, poll shows. And, Israelis vote in high-stakes election
entries.summary: Democrats are still holding a slight edge with Election Day a week away, according to a new NPR/PBS News/Marist poll. And, Israelis are casting their votes in an election that could change leadership.
entries.content:
Democrats Lead In NPR Poll, Preparations For Election Challenge, Israel Voting Begins

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

A new NPR/PBS News/Marist poll reveals that Democrats hold significant advantages in the midterm elections and are favored to gain control of the U.S. House. But there are also signs suggesting that a potential wave may be limited. The poll highlights key issues influencing voters; one in three Americans face financial hardships, and four in 10 say their personal finances are worsening. Preserving democracy resonates with Democrats and independents, while immigration ranks as the top issue for MAGA supporters.

  • 🎧 Democrats hold an 8-point advantage among likely voters on the generic congressional ballot, indicating a strong position, NPR's Domenico Montanaro tells Up First. President Trump remains unpopular. His approval rating sits at 40%, which is a slight improvement. While it seems unlikely that Democrats will lose the House, the Senate remains a toss-up. Montanaro says patience will be crucial for the outcomes of many races because it's unlikely the winners will be clear by election night, which is to be expected of vote counting in close elections.
  • ➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.

A federal judge today hears arguments in the Trump administration's bid to compel California to set aside ballots from voters it alleges may not be citizens. This comes after an appeals court last night declined the administration's request to get involved. 

  • 🎧 Trump announced yesterday that he is offering a $1 million reward for tips on voter fraud that lead to a conviction. The president has claimed fraud in every election he has participated in, prompting Democrats, election officials and good-governance groups to prepare for similar accusations, NPR's Eric McDaniel says. The White House says its efforts aim to secure elections. But McDaniel says credible evidence of voter fraud significant enough to affect election outcomes in the U.S. has never been found.
  • ➡️ With the elections a week away, Polymarket has already investigated "dozens" of bets on its prediction markets concerning the midterm elections, according to Shana Bautista, the company's head of global intelligence and investigations.

Israelis are voting today in an election that will shape their country's future. This marks the first time since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks that Israelis can choose their leaders. Voters will decide whether to keep Israel's far-right, longest-serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, or replace him with Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief promising more diplomacy and less extremism. Here's what you need to know about the leading candidates, the issues shaping the vote and what could happen next.

  • 🎧 NPR's Ruth Sherlock says a high voter turnout is expected, and many people casting their votes believe this is a critical election for the country's future. Israelis abroad have flown in to participate. At a polling station, Sherlock met Itamar Ariel, who believes that only Netanyahu can ensure Israel's security, even though the country faces problems. Others in the country believe Netanyahu should be voted out due to security failures. Those wanting change in leadership want an investigation into how the Oct. 7 attacks in Israel happened, which Netanyahu has blocked. Sherlock says by Wednesday morning, we should see which side secures the most seats in Parliament, but the vote count could continue for days, and the prime minister won't be determined until after days or possibly weeks of negotiations between the parties.

Life advice

Hours of screen time at your desk can turn you into a stiff, bleary-eyed version of yourself. Prolonged sitting can take a real toll, but a few smart habits can help reset your body and mind. Here are Life Kit's best strategies to help with the discomfort and health risks that can come from sitting at a desk all day.

  • 🧘 Walking for five minutes every 30 minutes helps combat fatigue, weight gain and joint pain, reducing the risk of chronic diseases like obesity, heart disease and cancer.
  • 🧘 If your back aches from slouching at your desk, rotate your spine to relieve stress and enhance flexibility by mimicking its natural movements.
  • 🧘 Fidgeting indicates a need to change your position. Pay attention to your body and switch between sitting, standing, reclining and moving.
  • 🧘 To relieve eye strain from screen time, stretch your eye muscles. Hold your arm straight in front of you, thumb pointing up. Move your arm in a big circle while keeping your head still and follow your thumb with your eyes.

Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

Picture show

Forget flying brooms. Cape Town is home to South Africa's real-world Hogwarts: the College of Magic. Every Saturday, almost 200 students ages 10 to 18 attend classes in a variety of things, including puppetry, mime and clowning, juggling, card tricks, illusions, mentalism, stage magic, theater production and escapology. In 1980, David Gore and a friend came up with the idea of starting a magic school. At the time, South Africa was grappling with apartheid, a brutal system of racial segregation. But from day one, the establishment was multiracial, even though state schools were still strictly segregated. Almost 50 years later, the College of Magic continues to stand out in a city that remains deeply divided along racial and economic lines. These photos capture how the school has turned young dreamers into magicians.

3 things to know before you go

  • Blue crabs in the Chesapeake Bay are threatened by invasive blue catfish. To tackle the problem, officials are creating kid-friendly catfish recipes that meet federal dietary requirements for school lunches in Maryland and Virginia.
  • Microsoft sent memos yesterday to about 60,000 employees, offering voluntary buyouts to further reduce its headcount. The offer is available to roughly one quarter of its workforce. (via KUOW)
  • The Archdiocese of New York has agreed to pay $800 million to settle claims from around 1,300 people who say they faced sexual abuse by clergy members and lay workers.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

entries.title: How Aldi is pushing down grocery prices
entries.summary: The German-owned chain's low prices are winning over shoppers — and pushing competitors to respond.
entries.content:
How Aldi is pushing down grocery prices

In the summer of 2020, I lived briefly in Ithaca, New York. It's the only time I've lived near Aldi, the grocery store known for low prices. I went twice, and I thought it was fine, but underwhelming. I appreciated the low prices, but it didn't have everything I needed. The store was small and a bit shabby.

I didn't know it yet, but those are the exact ingredients that have made Aldi the fastest-growing grocery chain in America. Per Bloomberg, Aldi plans to have more than 3,000 American locations by the end of 2028, which would be more than any other chain but Walmart. In 2024, Aldi generated some $29 billion in U.S. sales, which is more than Trader Joe's.

Aldi is a German company known for having low, low prices, and it deserves that reputation. Food reporter Deena Shanker told me that her experience comparison shopping over many months was that Aldi either matched Walmart on price or was a bit cheaper. Grocers like Wegmans and Kroger have announced defensive price reductions, and an analysis published in late 2023 of Lidl, another German grocer with a very similar model to Aldi's but fewer U.S. stores, found that grocery chains reduced their markups ~7 percent in areas where Lidl stores opened.

All to say: Aldi is disrupting the grocery business and actually lowering prices even as the cost of food—at restaurants and other grocery stores—goes up and up.

Maybe this sounds a bit humdrum. But I found it totally intriguing and perplexing, because…

  • Walmart and Costco's business models depend on low prices, too, and they can offer low prices by having huge stores, giant warehouses, and incredible economies of scale that allow them to pay less for Oreo's, baby carrots, and Jif peanut butter than other grocers. So how the heck is Aldi matching or beating them on price?
  • When a company disrupts a longstanding industry, it's typically a startup enabled by new technology—like Netflix using online streaming to disrupt Blockbuster and video rental. But Aldi is not staffed by futuristic robots. Its stores just look like grocery stores, and Aldi was founded 80 years ago, in post-war Germany. So what's going on?
  • One of the proudest achievements of America's capitalistic market economy is providing its citizens an abundance of increasingly affordable food. Somewhat famously, Soviet leader Boris Yeltsin toured a grocery store in Houston during the Cold War and was amazed that the average American enjoyed more variety than top Soviet politicians. From 1960 to 2019, Americans spent less and less of their income on food each year, even as they enjoyed more frequent restaurant meals, more sushi, and far better beer. But since the pandemic, food has become less affordable. Can American markets no longer provide cheap groceries? Did something break?

One necessary but not sufficient explanation for Aldi's low prices is that management is obsessed with efficiency and cutting unnecessary costs. There's no music in stores, because speakers (and licensing fees for muzak) cost money. The staff places products on shelves still in the cardboard boxes they were trucked in on, because artfully unpacking fruits, bread, and jerky sticks would mean higher labor costs. The shabbiness is intentional — it's the cost of cheaper groceries.

But other grocery chains are similarly obsessed with efficiency. Here's one of my favorite examples about Costco, courtesy of Zachary Crockett and The Hustle: "In another instance, reengineering a container of cashews from a circle to a square shape allowed Costco to stack more items in a single truck, reducing the number of shipments by 24,000 pallets per year. For shoppers, this meant cheaper nuts."

Instead, Aldi's disruptively low prices rely on two primary tactics:

  • Private label products: On Aldi shelves, you can find cookies that look a heck of a lot like Oreos and boxes of what sure seem like Ritz crackers. But they are "Benton's Chocolate Sandwich Cookies with Vanilla Filling" and "Savoritz Golden Round crackers." Both are made by Aldi, and therefore cost less, since Aldi doesn't have to pay Nabisco's markup and then add their own. More than 80 percent of Aldi products are these store-brand versions—aka private-label products or, in the case of look-alike Oreos,dupes.
  • Limited selection: When the Albrecht brothers took over their family's grocery store in 1946, they had a small store and limited funds for stocking the shelves. But this became their secret sauce: Stocking a very limited selection of items — just essentials like rice and eggs, and just one of each rather than a variety of brands, sizes, and versions — allowed them to keep prices low. They could buy in bulk, which is cheaper, and by not stocking niche products that sit on shelves for weeks or days, they saved even more by avoiding spoilage and limiting shelf space, storage areas, and rent or real-estate costs. Even as the brothers grew rich, they kept stores small and selection limited. This is less convenient— shoppers often have to visit another grocery store to grab things like white pepper that Aldi doesn't stock. But what Aldi does stock is cheaper.

Aldi's low prices made their stores very attractive during periods like the Great Recession and today's inflationary era. The Great Recession, especially, enabled their current growth. But if all Aldi offered was bargain prices in shabby stores, customers might flee to Costco, Kroger, or Whole Foods when the economy recovered.

So another key to Aldi's success is that it's fun. Aldi has a famously chaotic-good middle aisle with rotating buys like fun toys, German spätzle, and advent calendars that contain 24 festive cheeses. And its U.S. stores have expanded their offerings (a bit) to attract higher-income customers: Aldi doesn't just have the cheapest apples, but the cheapest honey crisp apples. Not just super-duper cheap wine but well-priced "premium" wine.

Instead of being a sad place to shop when you're low on cash, Aldi has more flea-market energy: a place anyone might go to hunt for good deals and fun finds. Aldi is beloved; many customers arecult-like in their devotion. In some cases, customers line up for new store openings like early iPhone releases.

My main takeaway from researching and analyzing Aldi for several weeks (foran episode of Gastronomics!) is that there's always something new under the sun. American grocery stores are a mature market. They seem pretty stable equilibrium-y. But they are dynamic and always changing. Aldi didn't need futuristic tech to disrupt the industry; just a strategy developed 80 years ago, then tweaked for the American market. In healthy markets, there's always a way in for new competitors.

My other takeaway is greater appreciation for the famous business idiom: "There are only two ways to make money in business: One is to bundle; the other is to unbundle."

The clearest example of bundling and unbundling is probably television. Cable companies bundled hundreds of TV channels together and charged one high fee for all of them. Then streaming services like Netflix made money by unbundling television — by allowing people to pay for just Netflix. Which felt liberating! For a few years. But now customers are annoyed about subscribing to so many streaming services. So streamers are teaming up to form bundles, like getting Disney, Hulu, and HBO Max all for one reduced price. Now, to make money, you gotta bundle.

Even the person who coined the phrase about bundling and unbundling didn't think it's literally the only way to make money. Still, I often failed to see (un)bundling as a powerful framework outside of the media industry. Until I realized that Aldi is unbundling the grocery store.

For a long time, grocery stores got more bundled. People once went to the baker, the butcher, and the greengrocer. Then the super market put all those things under one roof. And then Walmart, Target, and Costco created superstores where you could buy groceries and clothes and big-screen TVs.

Now Aldi is reversing this process by unbundling the grocery store. Not only does Aldi not have the big-screen TVs and dupes of Lululemon hoodies and pants, it doesn't even have everything on your grocery list. Aldi unbundled the part of the grocery business it can do super cheaply, and it intentionally locates Aldi stores near competitor grocery stores so shoppers can easily go grab the last few things on their list (the rest of the bundle).

With this in mind, I've started seeing bundling and unbundling at work in more and more industries. If you look closely at your own, I suspect you will, too.

My third takeaway is that I just didn't live in Ithaca long enough to grok Aldi. If I'd been there longer, I bet I would have made Aldi part of a multi-store strategy. I get it now! Aldi, please come to Colorado (where I live)!

At the start of this post, I asked three questions inspired by Aldi's expansion. The first two, which are about how Aldi achieved a comparative advantage, I feel like I've answered.

The third was whether the American economy can still deliver a bounty of affordable food. I think the way Aldi's growth pressured competitors to keep prices low shows that grocers are not the right target of our ire over food prices. But grocery stores are just one slice of the food world.

entries.title: Polymarket has investigated 'dozens' of election-related cases
entries.summary: The prediction market has hired a former FBI official to make sure political insiders don't use the platform for profit from confidential election information.
entries.content:
Polymarket has investigated 'dozens' of election-related cases

Polymarket has investigated "dozens" of bets on its prediction markets related to the midterm election, according to the company's head of global intelligence and investigations, Shana Bautista.

At least two of these Polymarket investigations have been referred to its regulator, the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, according to a person who is familiar with the probes, but not authorized to speak publicly about them.

These investigations into election insider trading and manipulation come as prediction market Polymarket — and its chief competitor Kalshi — have exploded in popularity over the past year. But the fast-growing industry also faces significant legal challenges from states and political pushback from lawmakers who argue betting on the outcome of elections poses serious risks to the democratic process.

In April, Kalshi banned and fined a handful of political candidates from betting on themselves. A month later, NPR reported that campaign staffers had made "thousands" using insider polling information to bet on their own candidates on platforms like Polymarket and PredictIt.

Polymarket's Bautista — a former FBI official and cryptocurrency analyst — told NPR her team of 16 and a new election surveillance system are actively policing election bets ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms.

"If you have information that you have a duty to protect, don't trade on it," Bautista said. "It's explicitly against our terms of use on both platforms, but also is against the law. If you decide that you are smarter and can do it, we will find you."

Bautista joined Polymarket in June. She oversees information gathered from both the U.S.-regulated version of Polymarket, which requires users to provide their real identities, and its bigger brother, Polymarket International, which is essentially unregulated and where trading can be done anonymously and with cryptocurrency. Despite this, Bautista said crypto trades are rarely completely anonymous.

"There's never been a case that we work where we haven't been able to identify, potentially, who these people are," Bautista said.

She said her election surveillance system pulls in "gigabytes" of data on each user from social media, Federal Election Commission data, cryptocurrency companies, banking partners, statistical models and other public information sources. If a user hits a certain number of internally-defined red flags, Bautista gets an alert on her phone.

"We're getting hundreds of alerts a day," Bautista said.

When asked about the specific detection criteria and thresholds, Bautista did not comment citing system security. But she said insider trading and market manipulation all look the same regardless of the financial market.

"We're looking at threat vectors and risk areas that have existed for decades in traditional markets," Bautista said. "But we recognize, too, that when it comes to prediction markets, we're seeing some of the old tried and known tactics, but being applied to a new vector through prediction markets."

Back in May, Kalshi, Polymarket's top rival, announced its own election surveillance system that also uses FEC data. Their system purportedly blocks any campaign staffer listed by the FEC from betting on an election. In July, Kalshi said it had blocked "dozens" of staffers from trading on elections, though at least one staffer told NPR they got around this. The staffer shared records of their recent trades and spoke to NPR on the condition of anonymity for fear of consequences for their future employment.

Prediction markets for elections are uniquely vulnerable to market manipulation and insider trading, said Rajiv Sethi, an economics professor at Barnard College at Columbia University, who has studied prediction markets for decades.

"[Election prediction markets] have the possibility of being a self-fulfilling prophecy," Sethi said. "Elections have the property that what one believes is going to happen can actually affect what happens if a candidate is thought to be losing momentum or the campaign is flagging."

Bautista said her Polymarket team and surveillance system is learning from past cases and putting their feet in the shoes of would-be insider traders and market manipulators.

"If I was worried about somebody trying to materially move an election market to make it look like one option was more likely to happen than the other and I identify a pattern where they're opening several different accounts and they're doing that in short bursts and I see device IDs consistent across different trades placed in short succession with new wallets across five or four different accounts," Bautista said. "If I were to work that case and then action that, the findings of that tactic go back into the process to create the detections."

As prediction markets have exploded in popularity over the last two years, the industry's federal regulator, the CFTC, has done little to police these new financial markets, largely leaving that work to the companies themselves.
